summary.text: A 24-year-old primigravida with no significant past medical history presented for her first obstetric visit at 8 weeks gestation with significant nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, anxiety and worry about an unplanned pregnancy. Prenatal vitamins and a doxylamine succinate-vitamin B6 combination pill were prescribed, routine prenatal labs were drawn, a dating ultrasound was unremarkable, and a real time PCBH consultation was completed.

She had frequent phone calls to the clinic about stress-related concerns including medication expense, completed treatment for bacterial vaginosis and chlamydia, hematuria on urinalysis, night sweats, congestion, tiredness and vaginal and pink discharge. She did not take any antiemetics during her prenatal course. She lost 3 pounds between the first and second clinic visits and subsequently maintained and gained weight until delivery.

She was seen 4 times for PCBH consultation during pregnancy, the last at 38 weeks, receiving education on the mind-body connection, relaxation response training and strategies including diaphragmatic breathing, prayerful meditation, music, comforting activities, mint or ginger tea/lozenges and meal pacing. NVPQOL category scores fell across six visits from 8w4d to 26w6d and PHQ-9 scores were below 5 on all but two assessments, with a highest score of 9.

Nausea, vomiting and stress decreased over later prenatal visits and at the final consultation, and inter-visit questions stopped at 29 weeks. She had an induction of labor at 40 weeks and a vaginal delivery of a male infant, an uncomplicated postpartum course, and was coping appropriately at 6-weeks postpartum.

article_limitations: The article has no figures and lists no supplements.
Dates of the two clinic visits are given only as gestational ages in Table 1; Table 1 scores are averages per item on a 0 to 7 scale.
The sentence about the delivery reads "health male infant"; infant health status is not recorded.
Discussion and background paragraphs describe the PCBH model and general statements, not patient facts.
Patient-raised possibilities (allergies, yeast infection, anemia) are recorded as possible/unconfirmed conditions; soda intake and the delivery hospital question are not recorded as clinical facts.
The treatment for bacterial vaginosis and chlamydia is recorded without drug names, which the source does not give.
